summary: A white paper summarizing the Distributed Interactive Simulation environment and its real-time nature, scope and networking requirements, as input for choosing IPng. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A paper describing the needs of big virtual training games, to help decide what the next Internet should do.

subtitle: Real-time, multicast, and reliability needs for military simulations.

tldr.problem: The Defense Modeling and Simulation community runs large, real-time distributed simulations that require precise timing, efficient multicast delivery, and guaranteed bandwidth across wide-area networks.
tldr.mechanism: This white paper articulates the network-layer requirements that IPng must support: low-latency responses (under 300 milliseconds), multicast groups with thousands of members, and resource reservation to guarantee performance.
tldr.outcome: IPng design was informed by these requirements, which motivated support for multicast and quality-of-service features in the protocol.

today: RFC 1667 is an Informational document from August 1994. It successfully influenced IPv6 design with its emphasis on multicast and quality-of-service requirements, both of which became core features of the protocol.

sections.title: Why DIS Matters for IPng
sections.content:
The Defense Modeling and Simulation community is a major user of packet networks and has significant requirements for the next-generation Internet Protocol (IPng). The protocols chosen for IPng will determine what networking technologies are widely available and affordable across commercial products. M&S applications that can rely on IPng's standard features will have advantages over those that need specialized, less-available protocols.

This paper specifies the network-layer requirements of Defense M&S applications as input to IPng design. The goal is to ensure that IPng supports multicasting, real-time response, and resource reservation as standard features, making these capabilities broadly available and cost-effective for the M&S community.
sections.plainLanguage: Virtual battles need a powerful Internet to work. If the new Internet doesn't help with these problems, the military will have to buy expensive special gear instead.

sections.title: Distributed Interactive Simulation
sections.content:
Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) is a system where simulation entities—tanks, aircraft, ships—run at geographically distant sites and exchange standardized protocol data units (PDUs) to coordinate their actions. A typical exercise might span hundreds of sites across the United States, Europe, and Korea, with tens of thousands of individual simulators. Some are computer-controlled forces, others are manned by humans.

Each moving entity generates one to two PDUs per second, typically 220 bytes in size but up to 1400 bytes, containing information like location, speed, weapons orientation, and radio frequency. The system must preserve the order of events and latency compatible with human reaction times to create a realistic combat simulation. Stationary entities send refresh traffic at rates as low as 0.2 PDUs per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine tanks, planes, and ships controlled from different buildings across the country, all sending messages about where they are and what they're doing. These messages have to arrive really fast and in the right order, like a video game that's played in real time.

sections.title: Real-Time Performance Requirements
sections.content:
DIS exercises require latency (end-to-end message delivery time) of 100 milliseconds for tightly-coupled simulations and 300 milliseconds for simulations with loose interactions. Delay variance (jitter) must be low enough that buffering at the receiving simulator does not exceed these latency targets. The reliability requirement is that 98 percent of all datagrams reach their intended destinations, with missing datagrams randomly distributed rather than in bursts.

These timing constraints ensure that simulated entities appear to interact naturally and in proper temporal order, even though they are geographically distant. A missile launched by one simulator must be visible to affected simulators within milliseconds, not seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages between simulators need to arrive within a third of a second, and almost all of them need to arrive at all. If they come too late or get lost in clumps, the battle simulation falls apart.

sections.title: Multicast and Group Management
sections.content:
Multicasting is essential to prevent network congestion when thousands of simulators exchange status updates. Each entity needs to receive only information relevant to it—for example, a tank only needs updates from nearby entities that could affect it in the simulation. The multicast capability must scale to support hundreds of sites and tens of thousands of platforms, with support for thousands of multicast groups, each potentially containing tens of thousands of members.

The system must allow hosts to join and leave multicast groups dynamically, with membership changes taking less than one second, at rates of hundreds of changes per second. The network layer should support both sender-initiated and receiver-initiated group joining, and ideally should leverage the multicast capabilities of underlying link technologies like broadcast LANs, Frame Relay, and ATM.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every simulator telling everyone else about itself, multicast lets each simulator tell only the simulators that care about it. It's like sending a group text instead of a billion individual messages.

sections.title: Resource Reservation and Bandwidth Guarantees
sections.content:
M&S community requires performance guarantees through resource reservation: IPng must support mechanisms to reserve bandwidth and other network resources in a multicast environment. These reservations guarantee network capacity for simulator-to-simulator communication across shared networks for the duration of the exercise. Without resource reservation, network congestion during a large exercise would degrade performance for all simulators.

The resource reservation mechanism should ensure that traffic without performance guarantees is rerouted, dropped, or blocked before reserved traffic is affected. Additionally, it is desirable for the reservation mechanism to support on-demand capacity when needed and for the network to feed back its loading status to applications, allowing graceful degradation of simulation fidelity when network resources become constrained.
sections.plainLanguage: The network needs a way to promise that certain messages will get through fast, so the battle simulation doesn't break when lots of traffic is on the network. Less important stuff gets slowed down or dropped instead.
